course: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01)
part_title: Lab 01 — Diagnose and Fix Context Overflow and Truncated Inputs
review_basis: Original checked-in local Module 19 slides 01–05 inspected visually; map.json and guides.mjs reviewed; full 74/74 local original asset audit passed.

scenes.title: Scenario and architecture
scenes.narration: You are investigating a generative AI contract assistant. The employee asks about the termination rights and notice period in a long contract, but the answer incorrectly says there is no termination clause. The right-hand sample response cites early pages about services, payment, and confidentiality. That tells us the model has responded, but not that it received the relevant evidence. Before changing the model, follow the architecture along the arrows. The synthetic contract, approximately one hundred pages in this example, is processed into chunks with metadata and stored for vector retrieval. The RAG application selects relevant chunks, assembles the final prompt, invokes a Bedrock-hosted foundation model, and returns a response with citations where available. Our expected behavior is an answer supported by the actual termination section near the end. Open the simulator's application and inspect the assembled prompt and the retrieved chunk list, then review CloudWatch logs for the corresponding model invocation. We need to distinguish three possible failures: the relevant chunk was never retrieved, the application dropped it while assembling context, or the model input or output limits cut off needed information. A model playground run with a small prompt cannot validate the application's full assembly path. Use the supplied synthetic document, record the request identifier and the model settings, and avoid pasting a real confidential contract into a test prompt. We will first gather evidence, then make the smallest correction, and finally prove that a long-document answer and its citations are complete.

scenes.title: Context concepts and failure branches
scenes.narration: This slide shows three separate failure branches, and it is important to choose between them using evidence instead of treating all missing answers as a token problem. Begin on the left with a long contract whose termination clause appears near page twenty in the simplified drawing. The middle example reserves one thousand five hundred tokens for output against an illustrative twelve-thousand-token model context budget while preparing ten thousand five hundred input tokens. That is an edge-of-budget example, not a universal Claude limit. An application can first truncate the prompt before it ever reaches Bedrock; the observable result is missing later sections, even when the API call succeeds. A second branch occurs when the assembled input exceeds the actual model's context requirement. The sample error on the lower right shows an invalid request with twelve thousand five hundred thirty-two input tokens against a twelve-thousand-token example limit. A third failure happens after successful admission: an output maxTokens stop produces an unfinished answer. Inspect the HTTP status and error body first, then look at the exact resolved input and any stop reason. A missing clause with HTTP success points toward retrieval or application assembly, not automatically an oversized model request. An invalid request points to admission limits; a response ending at the output limit points to generation truncation. Never fix the problem by silently discarding the last part of a legal contract. Record the model identifier, input size, output reservation, and response termination status before choosing a change.

scenes.title: Collect exact prompt and token evidence
scenes.narration: Now perform the investigation rather than guessing. Step one: capture the exact resolved prompt after system instructions, template variables, selected retrieval chunks, and the user question have all been assembled. The left console illustration highlights the termination clause near line eleven sixty-four of a synthetic contract, including the thirty-day written notice. Confirm that this section exists in the source, then ask whether it exists in the prompt actually sent to the model. Step two: count tokens using the model-supported tokenizer or token-counting API, not the number of characters returned by a command like word count. The middle example illustrates a Bedrock token counting command and an input-token result of twenty-eight thousand seven hundred forty-two. The saved evidence on the right records that count, a one-thousand-twenty-four-token output setting, total budget of twenty-nine thousand seven hundred sixty-six, the specific model identifier and a timestamp. Those figures come from a different illustrative request than the twelve-thousand-token branch on the previous slide; do not treat them as the same execution. Step three: compare input plus reserved output against the model's actual supported context window, accounting for the selected inference API. Step four: retain the request ID and source chunk identifiers so you can reproduce the failure. If the termination section never reached the prompt, investigate retrieval and assembly. If the request is over budget, reduce the context intentionally. If both are healthy, inspect response parsing and stop reasons. Keep the original source private and use synthetic test fixtures.

scenes.title: Fix prompt assembly and chunk selection
scenes.narration: The repair diagram has four stages. First, retrieve and rank chunks based on the user's question rather than simply taking the earliest pages. Here the relevant termination text is identified as chunk twenty-three, pages one hundred fifteen through one hundred twenty, and must be retained even though it is near the end of the long source. Second, assemble a bounded prompt. The example uses approximately three hundred tokens for system instructions, thirty-five hundred for selected context and fifty for the question, for an input of about three thousand eight hundred fifty tokens. Third, preserve provenance by including the chunk ID and page range beside the text so that citations can be checked. Fourth, invoke the model with explicit generation settings, shown with an illustrative maxTokens setting of eight hundred and temperature point two. In the application workbench, replace blind truncation with relevance-based chunk selection and a token-aware budget. Make sure the selected termination section appears in the resolved prompt before invoking the model. The lower-left prompt illustrates instructions to answer only from provided context and cite pages. The expected response on the lower right identifies thirty days of written notice and cites the corresponding chunk and page text. That is our positive confirmation that the evidence path was repaired. Do not assume higher maxTokens alone repairs absent source context, and do not change production retrieval settings without checking authorization filters and other questions.

scenes.title: Verify complete answers and prevent recurrence
scenes.narration: A single correct answer is not enough, so use the test matrix on the left. First run a long-document fixture whose termination clause is near the end. The correct output must identify the clause and notice period, with section number and a citation to the exact source span. The sample successful answer shows thirty days of written notice, but that is a synthetic test contract, not a legal interpretation of a real customer's agreement. Next test a short document with no termination clause. The correct behavior is an explicit answer such as not found in provided content, not an invented clause. Third test a middle-of-document question about the effective date to ensure the new relevance ranking did not damage ordinary retrieval. Finally exercise an over-budget prompt and require a controlled application error or safe reduction rather than silent truncation. The center shows the final prompt controls and a token summary: eighteen thousand seven hundred forty-two input tokens plus five hundred twelve reserved output tokens, within the two-hundred-thousand-token illustrative limit for that selected model. Check the actual model's supported limits in your deployment. The successful result includes a source file, page, and chunk identifier; validate those references against the text, not merely their presence. Record the results in your regression suite, monitor token budgets and missing-evidence responses, and remove synthetic test documents and saved prompts when the lab is complete. This gives us an evidence-based fix and a way to detect recurrence.
